text:
The wind off the Sawtooth Ridge did not howl; it possessed the dry, sibilant patience of broom bristles sweeping an empty stone floor. Arthur had been listening to it for three hours, his knees clicking a faint counterpoint as he descended the fire road toward the highway. He was sixty-two, an age at which a man’s body conducts a continuous inventory of its own diminishments. He walked alone because he lived alone, and he lived alone because, twelve years prior, his wife, Clara, had looked across a breakfast table littered with tangerine peels and told him, without malice, that he had the emotional availability of a sundial on a cloudy afternoon. 

He had come to the mountains to verify if he was still there at all.

He smelled the accident before he saw it—an incongruous tang of vaporized coolant and scorched rubber slicing through the scent of lodgepole pine. The guardrail on the hairpin turn above the ravine had been ironed flat, bowed outward over the drop. 

Arthur scrambled down the scree slope, his boots sending small avalanches of shale into the timber below. Halfway down, wedged violently between two Douglas firs that had halted its descent toward the glacial creek, sat a silver hatchback. It was inverted, its undercarriage exposed to the slate-gray sky like the pale belly of a dead trout. One rear wheel was still spinning, ticking faintly as a bent brake caliper grazed the rim. *Tick. Tick. Tick.*

"Hello?" Arthur called out. His voice sounded absurdly small in the vast, timbered amphitheater. 

He slid the remaining twenty feet and dropped onto the pine needles beside the crushed cab. The driver’s window had shattered into thousands of green-tinted pebbles that littered the forest floor like coarse salt. 

She was suspended upside down by her seatbelt, her head resting against the crumpled juncture of the A-pillar and the ceiling. She was perhaps thirty, wearing a mustard-colored cardigan over a white blouse. One sensible leather loafer had come off, lying near the gearshift. A dark ribbon of blood had tracked from her hairline and pooled in the hollow of her collarbone before drying. 

Arthur knelt, ignoring the bite of safety glass through his trousers. He reached through the jagged window and placed two fingers against the pale column of her neck. Her skin possessed the waning, borrowed warmth of a teacup left in an empty room, but there was no subcutaneous flutter. The stillness inside her was absolute, a profound mechanical cessation contrasting sharply with the ticking wheel above and the indifferent rush of the creek below.

He withdrew his hand and stood, his breath pluming white in the crisp October air. There was no phone service at the bottom of the ravine. He had to climb forty feet back up the loose shale before a single, tenuous bar of reception appeared. 

The dispatcher’s voice was crackly and distant. Arthur gave the mile marker from the junction. 

"Is the occupant responsive, sir?"

"No," Arthur said, looking down through the boughs at the dull silver lozenge of the car. "She’s gone."

"I need you to stay near the vehicle if it’s safe. State patrol is en route, but with the rockslide on Route 9, they’re looking at forty-five minutes. Can you stay?"

"Yes," Arthur said. "I have nowhere to be."

He descended a second time and sat upon a granite boulder three feet from the door. The rear wheel had finally stopped turning. In the absence of its ticking, the wilderness leaned inward, resuming its interrupted tenure. 

Arthur looked at the woman. A canvas tote bag had spilled its contents across the car's ceiling: a creased paperback, a tin of peppermint pastilles, a bundle of colored pencils, and an apple with a single, oxidized bruise. The artifacts of a Tuesday morning. She had woken up hours ago, chosen the mustard cardigan, locked her door, existed within a web of mundane anticipations—and then a patch of black ice, or a deer, had severed the thread.

"My name is Arthur," he said aloud. He felt foolish immediately, glancing up toward the highway. Yet the silence of the ravine was too heavy to bear uncontested; it demanded a human counterweight. 

"I used to calculate risk," he told her, watching a column of carpenter ants navigate the crumpled fender. To an ant, a catastrophe from above was merely new topography. "That was my profession. Mortality tables, statistical probabilities. When you spend your life looking at human existence from thirty thousand feet, everything flattens out. Tragedy becomes a decimal point. You begin to believe that because you can predict the aggregate, you are somehow exempt from the specific."

A breeze stirred the woman’s auburn hair, lifting a lock from her forehead and letting it fall back—a tiny pantomime of attention. 

"I had a brother," Arthur continued, his voice dropping into a conversational register. "Thomas. Younger by three years. When we were boys, we spent a summer at a lake in Michigan. One August afternoon, we swam out to an old wooden diving raft. Underneath, wedged between the barrels, we found a waterlogged box containing three glass marbles and a corroded pocket watch. We swore a blood oath never to reveal the cache, and to return every ten years." Arthur smiled faintly. "We never went back. Thomas died when he was twenty-six. Lymphoma. By the time the leaves were off the oaks, he was in a box of his own."

Arthur reached out and picked up the bruised apple that had rolled onto the pine needles, wiping the grit from its skin before setting it on the boulder beside him. 

"After my wife left, I drove up to that lake," he said. "Do you know what was there? A condominium complex. They had dredged the shallows for aluminum boat slips. The raft was gone, the shoreline corrected by a bulldozer. I stood in the parking lot and realized that the entire universe of that summer—the smell of wet pine, the sound of Thomas’s laugh—existed strictly within the six inches of gray matter between my ears. When I die, that afternoon dies a second time, and for good."

He looked at the woman’s hand, hanging loosely from the armrest. She wore a silver band with a turquoise stone on her thumb, her fingernails cut short and clean. Perhaps she played the cello, or worked with clay. A whole biography was locked behind her ribs, as inaccessible now as the bottom of the sea. 

"You had a version of the lake," Arthur said softly. "Some kitchen with yellow wallpaper. A joke only you and a college roommate understood. Where did it just go? That’s the question I could never fit into a spreadsheet. The sheer, extravagant waste of the data. You spend thirty years accumulating the specific texture of morning light through a curtain, and a patch of ice erases the archive."

The wind shifted, carrying a few stray flakes of snow. He thought of Clara in 1989, standing barefoot on a flooded Brooklyn subway platform during a downpour, laughing as a rat swam past like a miniature otter. He had loved her then with a ferocity that terrified him, because the actuary in him understood that anything of such high value represented a catastrophic potential loss. So he had insured himself against her. He rationed his affection, keeping a ledger of emotional reserves so that if the market crashed, he wouldn't be ruined. In doing so, he had caused the very bankruptcy he feared. 

"I was a coward," Arthur told the woman. There was a liberation in speaking to someone beyond the capacity to forgive or condemn. "I treated my life like a museum where you aren't allowed to touch the exhibits. I thought if I kept the room dark, the paintings wouldn't fade. It turns out they fade anyway, and you’ve just spent forty years sitting in the dark."

A massive raven landed on the upturned chassis, fixing Arthur with an obsidian eye before letting out a low, rattling croak. Arthur waved a gloved hand, but the bird merely hopped six inches to the left, waiting with an evolutionary patience that made sixty-two years look like the lifespan of a mayfly. 

He stood up, his joints aching, and stepped closer to the window. Snowflakes drifted through the broken glass, settling like tiny geometric stars in the woman’s hair. Without quite deciding to, Arthur reached in and laid his gloved palm gently over the back of her suspended hand. Her fingers were cold now, taking on the ambient temperature of the stone and iron around them. 

"I won't leave until they get here," he promised. "You’re already as far away as my brother. Further, maybe. At least I know his name."

He stayed like that as the minutes elongated, his hand resting lightly on hers. For the first time in longer than he could remember, he was not calculating the duration of an event, nor preparing for its conclusion. He was simply occupying the coordinate he had been given. 

From high above came the thin, warbling wail of a siren winding up the pass, followed by the growl of a heavy diesel engine downshifting on the grade. The raven launched itself off the car, gliding out into the gray void of the ravine. 

Minutes later, red and blue strobe lights painted the tops of the Douglas firs. Stones clattered down the slope as heavy boots breached the guardrail, accompanied by urgent, living voices. 

"Down here!" a voice shouted. "I see the tracks!"

Arthur gently removed his hand from the woman’s cold fingers. He nudged the bruised apple from the boulder into his vest pocket and stepped back into the ferns to give the men room. He stood watching their flashlights slice through the gathering snow, wondering what he would say to Clara if he called her tonight, and knowing, with a sudden, terrifying clarity, that the phone would ring in an empty kitchen if he waited too long.
